title: Dynamic Functional Connectivity as a complex random walk: Definitions and the dFCwalk toolbox
author: Arbabyazd, Lombardo, et al.

steps.title: Compute dFC matrix
steps.instruction: Convert a dFC stream (3‑D tensor or 2‑D matrix) into a recurrence matrix using the function dFCstream2dFC, which returns an F × F matrix where F is the number of frames. To change the analysis window size W or sliding step Δτ, first recompute the dFC stream with the desired parameters and then call dFCstream2dFC again.

steps.title: Calculate global dFC speed
steps.instruction: Define instantaneous global dFC speed as VdFC,W(t)=1−dFC(t,t+W). Use the high‑level function dFC_Speeds on the dFC matrix to obtain the typical speed and the full list of instantaneous speeds. With default parameters (Δf = 1) the syntax is: [typSpeed,Speeds]=dFC_Speeds(dFCstream2dFC(TS,W)).

steps.title: Oversample speeds with small sliding step
steps.instruction: Create a dFC stream with a sliding step Δτ smaller than the window size (e.g., Δτ = 1 TR) to obtain overlapping frames, then set Δf equal to the window size W so that each speed compares non‑overlapping windows. Example syntax: [typSpeed,Speeds]=dFC_Speeds(dFCstream2dFC(TS,W,1),W).

steps.title: Pool speeds across window sizes
steps.instruction: For each window size of interest compute a Speeds list with dFC_Speeds, then concatenate all lists: PooledSpeeds = [Speeds_W1; Speeds_W2; …; Speeds_Wk]. The median of PooledSpeeds is the pooled typical speed for the chosen range of windows.

steps.title: Plot dFC speed histogram
steps.instruction: Use BuildSpeedHistogram with a vector of instantaneous speeds (Speeds or PooledSpeeds) to draw a histogram. The function automatically adds bin‑by‑bin confidence intervals based on the Agresti‑and‑Coull binomial approximation; optional arguments allow control of bin numbers, centers, and output of numeric counts and intervals.

steps.title: Extract dFC increments for DFA
steps.instruction: Obtain instantaneous dFC increments (vdFC,W) by calling dFC_Speeds with Δf = 1 on a dFC stream computed with the smallest possible sliding step (Δτ = 1). Syntax: [~,Increments]=dFC_Speeds(dFCstream2dFC(TS,W,1),1).

steps.title: Perform detrended fluctuation analysis
steps.instruction: Apply the provided DFA_fun function to the Increments vector to estimate the DFA scaling exponent αDFA. Before interpreting αDFA, verify that the log‑log plot of fluctuation versus scale shows a clear linear region; optionally use the Bayesian model‑comparison procedure of Ton & Daffertshofer to confirm power‑law scaling.

steps.title: Optional alternative similarity metric
steps.instruction: If desired, replace the Pearson correlation used in dFC matrix construction with another similarity measure (e.g., Jaccard coefficient) by computing the similarity between UpperTri(FC(t1)) and UpperTri(FC(t2)) with the chosen metric.

description:
While structural connectivity refers to the existence of an anatomical connection between two neuronal regions –with the compilation of structural links between all pairs of anatomically interconnected regions known as the connectome
[44]–, the notion of functional connectivity (FC) intends to capture the existence of coordinated activity between two brain network nodes. Therefore, functional connectivity is necessarily way more flexible than the underlying structural connectome [37], being potentially the manifestation of collective emergent dynamics [9,30]. Notably, during the resting state (rs; [21]), the flexible sampling of a rich repertoire of possible dynamical states compatible with a given connectome [18,23] is expected to lead to a complex reconfiguration of FC along time, the characterization of which is the endeavor of the nascent field of “chronnectomics” [12]. Indeed, the brain is restless even at rest and rs FC continually fluctuates in a way which displays a nonrandom spatiotemporal organization [22]. There is growing evidence that such dynamic Functional Connectivity (dFC), in both rest and task conditions, can be used as a sensitive biomarker of the efficiency and flexibility of cognitive processing [7,14,43] as well as of pathological alterations of resting state dynamics [8,15,28]. To the growth in the number of dFC studies, has corresponded an analogous inflation in the number of possible methods to extract and quantitatively parameterize dFC from fMRI data or other time-series of neural activity (such as EEG, MEG, fNIRS…). We invite the reader to refer to e.g. Preti et al. [40] for a non-exhaustive review. Many approaches have tried to characterize “states of FC” that would be visited at different times by the evolution of FC.
